title: Stored physical samples may be retained beyond their authorized lifecycle
description: This flow places a physical biological sample into freezer storage. If retention schedules, destruction triggers, or end-of-use criteria are not enforced for stored specimens, the sample may remain available beyond the period justified by the original collection or storage purpose.
assumptions: Assumes the physical sample is personal data or personal material linked, or linkable, to a data subject and that its storage lifecycle is governed by protocol, policy, consent, or legal limits.
uncertainty_note: Best-effort mapping: PA12.01 clearly fits the storage context, but the exact LINDDUN Pro Dd tree-node id for over-retention may differ from Dd.1 in your catalog.

title: Insufficient physical/logical access control over stored samples could enable unauthorized handling
description: Once the wet lab transfers the physical sample into storage, inadequate access restrictions on freezers, racks, logs, or retrieval procedures could allow unauthorized personnel to access, inspect, move, or extract information from the specimen, undermining proper stewardship of personal biological material.
assumptions: Assumes samples are stored in a controlled repository where access should be restricted based on role, study authorization, or chain-of-custody requirements.
uncertainty_note: PANOPTIC PA04.01 is applicable to the storage endpoint, but the nearest LINDDUN Pro Nc tree-node id is best-effort; use your local threat-tree taxonomy if it has a more specific node for inadequate access control.

title: Storage may proceed without sufficient agreed usage restrictions for downstream handling of the sample
description: By placing the physical sample into storage for later access and use, the organization creates downstream opportunities for further processing or sharing. If the repository lacks adequate usage restrictions, material transfer constraints, or stewardship rules tied to the specimen, later handling may exceed what was authorized for the data subject.
assumptions: Assumes stored samples can later be retrieved, analyzed, transferred, or repurposed by internal or external parties, and such downstream use should be constrained by protocol, consent, contract, or governance controls.
uncertainty_note: This is a governance-oriented privacy threat inferred from the storage step; applicability depends on whether downstream sample use is actually possible from this repository and subject to restrictions.

title: Pseudo-identifier assignment may still enable later re-identification
description: This flow sends a de-identified ID from LIMS to the Wet Lab for use with the sample. Even though the identifier is intended to be de-identified, assigning and propagating a persistent pseudo-identifier creates a privacy risk if the Wet Lab or another party can later correlate it with other records or a re-identification key.
assumptions: Assumes the returned ID is a stable pseudo-identifier linked to sample metadata and that some party in the ecosystem may retain means to map it back to the individual.
uncertainty_note: Best fit PANOPTIC action is PA05.02.02 because the flow distributes a pseudo-identifier. The exact LINDDUN Pro tree node for identifier assignment is approximate.

title: De-identified ID may be insufficiently de-identified for downstream handling
description: The flow is explicitly about sending a de-identified ID to the Wet Lab. If the de-identification is weak, reversible, unique in context, or combined with accompanying sample metadata, the Wet Lab may still be able to identify or single out the data subject, defeating the intended privacy protection.
assumptions: Assumes the Wet Lab receives or can access contextual metadata beyond the bare identifier, or that the identifier/token design is not robust against linkage.
uncertainty_note: This is grounded in the flow's explicit mention of a de-identified ID; applicability depends on the actual de-identification scheme and what auxiliary data the Wet Lab can access.

title: Downstream responsibilities for handling the de-identified ID may be insufficiently communicated
description: LIMS is sharing a de-identified sample ID with the Wet Lab for downstream use. If the Wet Lab's obligations for permissible use, re-identification prohibition, safeguarding, and onward disclosure are not clearly communicated and enforced, the downstream recipient may mishandle the identifier and associated metadata.
assumptions: Assumes this flow represents a transfer to a separate operational team or trust boundary where stewardship obligations are not automatically guaranteed.
uncertainty_note: This threat depends on governance context; if the Wet Lab is fully governed by explicit SOPs, contracts, or equivalent controls, the risk may be reduced.

title: Exposure of sample metadata or de-identified ID during sharing could enable linkage
description: The flow shares sample metadata and the de-identified ID from LIMS to the Wet Lab. If this transfer is exposed to unauthorized recipients, even a de-identified identifier plus metadata may become linkable to a person or sample source, revealing information that should remain protected.
assumptions: Assumes unauthorized parties could gain visibility into the shared flow through overbroad access, accidental disclosure, or insecure transmission/channel configuration.
uncertainty_note: Mapped to sharing exposure because the risk arises from making the identifier/metadata accessible beyond intended recipients; exact tree node is approximate.

title: Stored raw sequence data may be retained beyond its necessary lifecycle
description: This flow sends digital raw sequence data into the cluster filesystem for storage. Because the action is explicitly storage-oriented, a plausible privacy threat is that the data remains in the filesystem after the purpose for which it was collected or processed has ended, increasing the chance of future unauthorized use, disclosure, or reuse of highly sensitive sequence data.
assumptions: Assumes the sequence data is personal or reasonably linkable to an individual and that retention limits or disposal triggers should apply.
uncertainty_note: Applies only if retention/destruction controls are not enforced for this storage location; the flow alone does not prove over-retention.

title: Cluster filesystem storage may have insufficient access controls for sensitive sequence data
description: The flow places raw sequence data into a shared cluster filesystem. If access controls on that datastore are insufficient, unauthorized internal users, adjacent projects, or service accounts could access personal genomic data beyond intended purposes.
assumptions: Assumes the cluster filesystem is shared or broadly reachable and stores sensitive sequence data whose access should be limited by role, project, or study.
uncertainty_note: The privacy threat is genuine for this storage flow, but the exact control weakness is not evidenced from the flow description alone; tree node is a best-effort mapping.

title: Sequence data may be stored or transferred to storage without adequate encryption protections
description: This flow transfers digital raw sequence data to persistent storage. If encryption in transit to the cluster filesystem or encryption at rest within the datastore is absent or weak, the confidentiality of highly sensitive sequence data may be compromised, enabling privacy harm through later access or exposure.
assumptions: Assumes sequence data is sensitive and the environment requires encryption either in transit, at rest, or both.
uncertainty_note: The flow description does not state whether encryption is missing; this is a best-effort PANOPTIC insecurity threat grounded in the storage transfer.

title: Raw sequence data may be stored without sufficient de-identification
description: Digital raw sequence data is inherently highly identifying and may permit re-identification or sensitive inference even when obvious identifiers are removed. Storing the raw data in the cluster filesystem without sufficient de-identification or minimization can create downstream disclosure and misuse risks.
assumptions: Assumes the stored sequence data pertains to human subjects or otherwise linkable individuals and that de-identification or minimization is expected before broader storage access.
uncertainty_note: This is strongly plausible for human genomic raw data, but applicability depends on whether the dataset is human and whether this storage tier is intended for identifiable raw data.

title: Sensitive information can be derived from raw sequence data during compute processing
description: This flow delivers digital raw sequence data from the cluster filesystem to compute nodes specifically so the nodes can operate on it and transform it into objective-specific data. Raw sequence data can enable inference of new sensitive attributes about data subjects, including genetic characteristics, health-related traits, ancestry, or other sensitive biological findings beyond the originally stored representation.
assumptions: Assumes the sequence data is human or otherwise linked to identifiable or potentially identifiable data subjects, and that the compute task includes analytical transformation rather than mere transport or storage.
uncertainty_note: Best-fit LINDDUN tree node selected for a disclosure/content-unawareness style processing threat; exact Dd node mapping may vary in LINDDUN Pro.

title: Compute processing may re-identify data subjects from sequence data
description: Even if the sequence data is treated as de-identified or pseudonymized in storage, transferring it to compute nodes for analysis can enable re-association with an individual because genomic sequence data is inherently identifying or can be matched with other datasets. The privacy threat materializes at the compute node where the identification inference occurs.
assumptions: Assumes sequence data concerns persons and that auxiliary data, metadata, or analytical methods available to compute nodes could support linkage back to a specific individual.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is a best-effort identification mapping; genomic identifiability depends on context, metadata, and available linkage sources.

title: Sequence data may be insufficiently de-identified before analysis on compute nodes
description: This flow moves raw sequence data to compute nodes for transformation. If identifiers are removed but the underlying sequence remains sufficiently unique, the data may still permit identification or sensitive inference. Sending such data for analysis without adequate de-identification creates a privacy threat at the receiving compute environment.
assumptions: Assumes the system intends or represents the sequence data as de-identified, pseudonymized, or otherwise privacy-protected before downstream analysis.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on whether de-identification is expected in this architecture; if raw identifiable sequence data is intentionally processed under proper authority, this threat may be less applicable.

title: Compute transformation may process sequence data beyond the permitted scope
description: The stated purpose is to transform raw sequence data into objective-specific data. A privacy threat exists if the compute nodes perform broader analytics than necessary for that objective, such as extracting additional traits, performing secondary research, or generating outputs not covered by the authorized purpose or agreed limits.
assumptions: Assumes there are purpose limitations, study constraints, policy limits, consent boundaries, or contractual restrictions governing use of the sequence data.
uncertainty_note: This is a purpose-limitation threat inferred from the stated objective-specific transformation; exact LINDDUN node is best-effort.

title: Compute nodes may be unvetted recipients of raw sequence data
description: The cluster filesystem sends raw sequence data to compute nodes for analysis. If the legitimacy, trust posture, tenancy, or authorization status of those compute nodes has not been adequately assessed, sensitive personal data may be provided to recipients that are not sufficiently trustworthy for this class of data.
assumptions: Assumes the compute environment could be elastic, multi-tenant, federated, administered by distinct operators, or otherwise not automatically trusted merely because it is technically reachable.
uncertainty_note: Applies most strongly where compute nodes are dynamically provisioned, shared, or externally managed.

title: Downstream compute processing practices may be insufficiently vetted
description: Beyond trusting the compute nodes as recipients, the specific processing they perform on raw sequence data may not be adequately assessed. The transformation pipeline could retain intermediate files, create broader analytical outputs, or trigger additional downstream uses that exceed privacy expectations.
assumptions: Assumes downstream jobs, workflows, containers, or analysts operating on the compute nodes may have privacy-relevant behavior not fully reviewed or constrained.
uncertainty_note: Best-fit non-compliance/node mapping; this threat is about insufficient review of downstream handling rather than a demonstrated policy breach.

title: Usage restrictions for compute-side processing may be insufficient or absent
description: Raw sequence data is sent to compute nodes for transformation, but if data use agreements, job constraints, or processing restrictions are not defined with enough precision, the receiving environment may analyze the data for additional purposes or handle outputs in ways that exceed approved use.
assumptions: Assumes some organizational, contractual, study, or regulatory restrictions should govern compute-side use of the sequence data.
uncertainty_note: Threat depends on the existence of expected usage restrictions; exact Nc node is best-effort.

title: Insufficient access controls on compute nodes could expose incoming raw sequence data
description: Once the raw sequence data reaches compute nodes, weak or overly broad access controls on those nodes, their mounted storage paths, job contexts, or service accounts could allow unauthorized parties to access highly sensitive sequence information.
assumptions: Assumes compute nodes host multiple users, services, jobs, or administrative roles, creating the possibility of unauthorized access after the transfer completes.
uncertainty_note: This threat is located at the receiving compute environment rather than on the data store because the flow places the data into that environment.

title: Misconfigured permissions on compute infrastructure could permit improper handling of sequence data
description: The transfer of raw sequence data to compute nodes creates privacy risk if file permissions, mount permissions, container permissions, or role assignments on the receiving environment are misconfigured, enabling copying, secondary disclosure, or unauthorized processing of the data.
assumptions: Assumes the compute platform relies on configurable OS, cluster, filesystem, or orchestration permissions that can be set too broadly.
uncertainty_note: Best-fit non-compliance node; exact LINDDUN Pro subtree for permission misconfiguration may differ.

description: This flow copies context-relevant research data from the cluster filesystem into a data delivery DMZ specifically to make it available for delivery. Placing personal or potentially re-identifiable research data in a DMZ increases the risk that the data becomes discoverable or accessible beyond the intended audience if the delivery area is broadly reachable, insufficiently segmented, or incorrectly published.
assumptions: Assumes the context-relevant research data includes personal data or data that can be linked to individuals, and that the DMZ is a more exposed distribution environment than the source filesystem.
uncertainty_note: PANOPTIC fit is strong for sharing/exposure, but the exact LINDDUN Pro tree node id is uncertain; 'PA' is a placeholder because the applicable detailed node id was not provided in the prompt.

title: Sharing to the DMZ may exceed approved research-data sharing scope
description: Moving generated research data into the data delivery DMZ for downstream delivery could constitute sharing beyond the limits established by participant consent, data-use terms, IRB approval, or other source constraints. The privacy threat arises if data prepared for delivery includes fields, records, or recipients outside the authorized sharing scope.
assumptions: Assumes the research data is subject to contractual, ethical, or regulatory sharing constraints and that the DMZ is used for downstream disclosure to recipients.
uncertainty_note: This depends on whether applicable sharing restrictions exist for this dataset. The exact LINDDUN Pro threat-tree node id is uncertain; 'SV' is a best-effort placeholder, not a verified node id.

title: Downstream recipients reached via the delivery DMZ may be insufficiently vetted
description: Because this flow populates a delivery environment intended for external distribution, a privacy threat exists if the legitimacy, authorization, or trustworthiness of the eventual recipients has not been adequately assessed before data is made available there. This can result in disclosure of research data to inappropriate or excessive recipients.
assumptions: Assumes the DMZ supports delivery to downstream consumers outside the immediate trusted processing boundary.
uncertainty_note: The PANOPTIC mapping is plausible for a delivery flow, but recipient-vetting controls are not described explicitly. The tree node id is a best-effort approximation.

title: Usage restrictions for delivered research data may be insufficient or absent

Without such controls, recipients may reuse, redistribute, or retain the data in privacy-harmful ways.

uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on governance arrangements for downstream delivery. The exact LINDDUN Pro tree node id is uncertain.

title: Access controls on the delivery DMZ may be insufficient for staged research data
description: This flow places research data into a DMZ for delivery. If the delivery datastore lacks sufficiently restrictive authorization, segregation, or least-privilege controls, unauthorized parties may access the staged data, causing a privacy breach.
assumptions: Assumes the DMZ is exposed to a broader set of systems, operators, or networks than the source filesystem.
uncertainty_note: Strong privacy relevance, but the exact LINDDUN Pro tree node id is uncertain; 'SEC' is only a best-effort placeholder.

title: Data transferred or stored for delivery may lack adequate encryption
description: Sending research data from the cluster filesystem to the delivery DMZ creates privacy risk if the transfer path or the DMZ storage does not use adequate encryption. This may permit interception or unauthorized recovery of personal or sensitive research data during staging for delivery.
assumptions: Assumes the transferred dataset contains personal or sensitive information and that encryption requirements apply in transit and/or at rest.
uncertainty_note: The flow description does not specify transport or storage protections. The exact tree node id is uncertain.

title: DNA Store may fulfill sample requests for an insufficiently vetted recipient
description: This flow sends a physical sample request from an NCCoE Researcher to the DNA Store so the store can release a biospecimen for sequencing. A privacy threat exists if the DNA Store does not adequately verify the requester's authority, role, protocol approval, and need-to-know before honoring the request, causing a biological sample linked to a data subject to be disclosed for an unauthorized or inappropriate downstream use.
assumptions: Assumes the request contains enough subject/sample identifiers to locate a specific specimen and that release of the specimen enables access to associated personal or genomic information downstream.

title: DNA Store may release samples without sufficient usage restrictions on downstream handling

If data use terms, handling constraints, destruction requirements, or resequencing/recontact restrictions are absent or insufficient, the specimen can be used beyond agreed privacy boundaries.
assumptions: Assumes the specimen is governed by protocol, consent, or data-use restrictions that should travel with the request and release decision.
uncertainty_note: This is grounded in the request flow because release authorization should enforce downstream stewardship constraints, but evidence of actual agreements is not provided. Tree node is best-effort and approximate for non-compliance.

title: Sample request can trigger collection/use of a biological sample beyond the approved scope
description: This flow operationalizes access to a biological specimen stored in the DNA Store. A privacy threat exists if the requested sample retrieval and shipment for sequencing causes biological material to be collected, re-collected, or used for a purpose outside the scope originally authorized by the data subject or governing protocol, especially where the specimen enables highly sensitive genomic analysis.
assumptions: Assumes the stored specimen originated from a human data subject and that sequencing constitutes a privacy-relevant use of the biological sample.
uncertainty_note: PANOPTIC PA03.11 applies because the flow concerns a biological sample, but this specific flow is a request for release from storage rather than initial specimen collection; applicability is therefore contextual. LINDDUN tree node is approximate.

description: This flow transfers a physical biological sample from the DNA Store to the NCCoE Researcher. A genuine privacy threat exists if the store releases the sample without adequately assessing whether the requesting researcher is authorized and appropriate to receive this specimen, since a biological sample can enable sensitive downstream analysis and handling.
assumptions: Assumes the sample is linked or linkable to a data subject and that release depends on an authorization/vetting decision by the DNA Store or its operators.
uncertainty_note: Best-fit PANOPTIC activity is PA06.04 (unvetted recipients). The chosen LINDDUN tree node is a best-effort mapping for disclosure-related downstream release risk; exact node may vary depending on the project's threat-tree version.

title: Insufficient usage restrictions may govern researcher handling of the retrieved biological sample
description: When the NCCoE Researcher retrieves the physical sample, privacy risk arises if applicable data/material use agreements or stewardship restrictions are missing or too weak. Without clear restrictions on permissible use, retention, sharing, and destruction, the sample may be processed beyond the intended scope.
assumptions: Assumes the sample is subject to consent, protocol, contractual, or governance restrictions that should constrain researcher handling after retrieval.
uncertainty_note: The threat is located at the receiving researcher because the privacy risk materializes in downstream handling. The LINDDUN node is an approximate best-fit for non-compliance / policy-governance failure.

title: Sharing the physical sample with the researcher may exceed the scope established for the specimen

In that case, the downstream disclosure of the specimen is out of scope even if the sample was lawfully stored.

title: Researcher may deviate from usage restrictions attached to the biological sample

Because a biological specimen can reveal highly sensitive information, such deviation creates a substantial privacy risk tied to this disclosure flow.

uncertainty_note: This is a downstream misuse/compliance threat enabled by the transfer rather than evidence that violation is already occurring. Tree-node mapping is approximate.

uncertainty_note: Applies if the retrieval mechanism allows broader discoverability than intended. Tree node is approximate.

title: Clinician analysis may enable multi-source profiling of the patient
description: The flow explicitly says the Clinician retrieves the provided data with additional input and analysis. Combining context-relevant research data with other clinical sources can assemble a richer profile of the patient than either source alone, increasing linkability and the ability to correlate records across contexts.
assumptions: Assumes the clinician has access to additional patient data sources and the transferred data can be linked at the individual level.
uncertainty_note: This is grounded in the stated 'additional input and analysis'; however, whether it becomes a privacy threat depends on whether such cross-context profiling exceeds expectations or permissions. Tree node is a best-effort approximate mapping.

title: Clinician analysis may derive additional sensitive information from the shared data
description: The clinician is expected to perform additional input and analysis on context-relevant research data. That analysis can produce new sensitive inferences, such as disease susceptibility, hereditary implications, or family-related risk information, beyond what was explicitly conveyed in the original data transfer.
assumptions: Assumes the dataset includes genetic or genomics-related information from which additional health-related inferences can be drawn.
uncertainty_note: The threat is strongly supported by the flow description's reference to additional analysis. Exact LINDDUN node is approximate.

title: Residual genomic data recoverable after device decommissioning
description: The flow concerns writing decommissioning actions to privacy-relevant wet lab devices so they can be retired or resold. A privacy threat exists if sanitization is incomplete or ineffective, leaving genomic or associated personal data partially recoverable from device storage, logs, caches, firmware, or attached media after decommissioning.
assumptions: Wet lab devices may retain privacy-relevant data locally (e.g., run files, sample metadata, logs, temporary files, calibration histories, or embedded storage) and may be resold or transferred outside the original trust boundary.
uncertainty_note: Best-fit LINDDUN Pro node selected as a retention/destruction disclosure threat; exact tree node mapping may vary because PANOPTIC grounds this directly in decommissioning rather than a standard LINDDUN DFD-position interaction.

title: Personal data retained on device beyond end of lifecycle
description: If the decommissioning process does not actually remove stored genomic data and related metadata at the end of the device lifecycle, the device continues retaining personal information after its intended use has concluded. This creates a privacy risk even before any subsequent purchaser or third party accesses the device.
assumptions: The devices store or buffer personal/genomic data or metadata locally long enough for retention at end-of-life to be meaningful.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is a best-effort non-compliance/retention mapping; exact LINDDUN Pro node id may differ.

title: Decommissioning responsibilities for downstream recipients are not sufficiently assured
description: Because the flow explicitly contemplates resale of devices, a privacy threat exists if downstream recipients are not clearly bound to residual-data handling and stewardship responsibilities. Absent or weak communication of those responsibilities can lead to improper handling of remaining genomic data artifacts.
assumptions: Devices may be transferred to resellers, refurbishers, recyclers, or buyers who could encounter residual data if sanitization is incomplete.
uncertainty_note: Applicable only if resale/transfer occurs without clear downstream stewardship obligations; LINDDUN tree node is best-effort because this PANOPTIC quality-assurance issue does not map cleanly to a single published LINDDUN Pro node.

title: Residual genomic data recoverable on acquired wet lab devices
description: A device acquired from a manufacturer or refurbisher may retain recoverable genomic or related personal data from prior use if sanitization/destruction was incomplete. When the device enters the environment, previously stored data could be exposed to the acquiring organization, creating a disclosure risk tied to improper destruction at the end of the prior lifecycle.
assumptions: The wet lab devices can store digital data locally (e.g., runs, logs, cached files, metadata) and may have been previously used before acquisition or refurbishment.
uncertainty_note: Best-fit PANOPTIC activity is clear from the flow description, but the exact LINDDUN Pro Dd tree node id is approximate because the PANOPTIC-to-tree mapping for improper destruction on an acquisition flow is not explicit.

title: Device supplier or refurbisher legitimacy not adequately vetted before acquisition
description: If the acquisition specialist does not adequately assess the trustworthiness and privacy posture of the manufacturer or refurbisher, devices may be obtained from parties that mishandle residual personal data or fail to apply sound sanitization practices. This creates a privacy compliance and stewardship risk for any personal data remaining on the devices.
assumptions: Acquisition may involve third-party manufacturers or refurbishers and the procurement process may not consistently verify privacy-preserving refurbishment practices.
uncertainty_note: Mapped to unvetted recipients/sources in PANOPTIC as a procurement-context quality/compliance issue; the closest Nc tree node is approximate.

title: Downstream refurbishment practices not sufficiently assessed
description: The procurement flow may rely on claims that devices were refurbished according to privacy best practices without validating the actual downstream data handling and sanitization procedures. If those downstream practices are weak, residual personal data can persist and be inappropriately transferred with the device.
assumptions: Refurbishment is performed by an external party and the acquisition decision may be based on contractual or marketing claims rather than technical validation of sanitization processes.
uncertainty_note: This is a strong contextual fit to the described privacy-best-practices concern, but the selected Nc tree node id is a best-effort approximation.

title: Supplier or refurbisher privacy certification or standards claims may be inaccurate
description: A manufacturer or refurbisher may claim adherence to privacy best practices, sanitization standards, or certification requirements without actually conforming to them. Acquiring devices based on such inaccurate claims can introduce residual personal data and associated privacy harms into the environment.
assumptions: Procurement decisions may rely on asserted conformity statements, certifications, or privacy/security attestations from suppliers.
uncertainty_note: Applicable only where acquisition relies on claimed conformance or certification; included as conditional because the flow description references refurbishment according to privacy best practices but not an explicit certification.
